alignment.note: Greek ἀπ᾽ ἀγορᾶς, Syriac ܘܡܢ ܫܘܩܐ (the conjunction is prefixed to the preposition), and Latin a foro all render 'from the marketplace'; the Syriac compresses 'and from' into a single proclitic ܘܡܢ.
The postpositive Greek δέ ('now/and') is a discourse connective with no separate equivalent in either the Peshitta or the Vulgate, both of which lack a corresponding particle here.

The Greek temporal clause ὅταν ἔλθωσιν ('whenever they come [back]') is wholly absent from both the Peshitta and the Vulgate, which proceed directly to the conditional clause; this is a substantive omission of the verbal action of returning from the market.

Greek ἐὰν μή ('unless') is rendered by the single Syriac particle ܐܠܐ and by Latin nisi; all three express the same negative conditional, with Greek using a two-word construction against the single-lexeme idioms of the versions.

Greek βαπτίσωνται is aorist middle subjunctive ('they wash themselves'); the Peshitta ܥܡܕܝܢ is a present participle and the Vulgate baptizentur a present passive subjunctive, differing in voice and aspect but agreeing in sense of ritual washing.

Greek ἐσθίουσιν and Syriac ܠܥܣܝܢ render 'they eat'; the Vulgate comedunt carries the same sense, and the following colon (idx 7) marks the major sense-break that the Greek expresses with its mid-stop punctuation.

The coordinating conjunction (Greek καί, Latin et) introduces the second clause; the Peshitta marks the same coordination by prefixing the proclitic ܘ to the following noun ܘܣܓܝܐܬܐ rather than with a separate word.

Greek ἄλλα πολλά ('many other things') places the substantive adjective before the quantifier; the Syriac ܘܣܓܝܐܬܐ ܐܚܪܢܝܬܐ and Latin alia multa preserve the pair but with internal word-order differences typical of each language's adjectival sequencing.

Greek ἐστιν (3rd sg.) and Latin sunt (3rd pl.) differ in number because Greek treats the neuter plural subject ἄλλα πολλά with a singular verb (Attic concord); the Syriac existential particle ܐܝܬ is number-neutral, so all three are semantically equivalent.

Greek παρέλαβον is active ('which they received [as tradition]'); the Vulgate tradita sunt is passive ('which were handed down'), inverting the diathesis, while the Syriac ܕܩܒܠܘ retains the active 'which they received.'
The Vulgate adds the dative pronoun illis ('to them'), making explicit the recipients of the tradition; neither the Greek nor the Syriac supplies an overt indirect object here.

Greek infinitive κρατεῖν ('to hold/keep') is matched by the Vulgate infinitive servare; the Syriac ܕܢܛܪܘܢ uses a finite imperfect with relative ܕ ('that they should keep'), a construction-level difference rendering the same purposive sense.
Greek βαπτισμούς ('washings'), Syriac ܡܥܡܘܕܝܬܐ (from the root ʿ-m-d, the same root as 'baptize'), and Latin baptismata all denote ritual ablutions of vessels.
The conjunction (Greek καί, Latin et) is rendered in Syriac by the proclitic ܘ prefixed to the following noun ܘܕܩܣܛܐ rather than as an independent word.

Greek ξεστῶν is a Latin loanword (sextarius, a liquid measure/pot); the Vulgate urceorum ('pitchers') and the Syriac ܕܩܣܛܐ (a loan from Latin sextus/Greek ξέστης) all denote small measuring vessels, with each tradition selecting its own culturally familiar term.
Coordination expressed by Greek καί and Latin et; the Syriac prefixes the proclitic ܘ to the following noun-phrase ܘܕܡܐܢܝ ܢܚܫܐ.

Greek χαλκίων ('copper utensils') is rendered by the Syriac two-word genitive phrase ܕܡܐܢܝ ܢܚܫܐ ('vessels of bronze/copper') and the Latin æramentorum ('bronze wares'); the Syriac unpacks the single Greek noun into an explicit construct chain.
The final coordinating conjunction (Greek καί, Latin et) is again represented in Syriac only by the proclitic ܘ attached to ܘܕܥܪܣܬܐ.

Greek κλινῶν denotes 'dining couches' (the gloss reflects Greco-Roman triclinium custom); the Syriac ܕܥܪܣܬܐ and Latin lectorum both mean 'beds/couches.' Many witnesses omit this final clause about couches; its presence here aligns the three traditions, with the Vulgate closing on a colon (idx 25).
